sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Every Go interviewer opens with core type questions to separate people who have read Go syntax from people who understand the runtime model. Knowing the difference between value and reference semantics, how zero values eliminate null-pointer surprises, and when addressability applies shows you think in Go rather than translating from another language.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Think of Go's type system as two worlds: value types (structs, arrays, primitives) that are copied on assignment, and reference types (slices, maps, channels, pointers, functions) that carry an internal pointer so copies share the same underlying data. Every variable is always initialised to its zero value — there is no uninitialised memory in Go. Pointers are just typed integer addresses; addressability determines whether you can take one.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
• Value vs reference semantics: structs are copied; slices/maps share backing data.
• Zero values: int→0, bool→false, string→"", pointer/slice/map/chan/func→nil.
• iota: untyped integer counter reset to 0 in each const block; enables typed enumerations.
• Type assertions: x.(T) panics if wrong type; two-value form x.(T) is safe.
• Type switches: switch v := i.(type) dispatches on runtime concrete type.
• Named return values: named results are pre-declared locals; bare return returns them — use sparingly, useful in defer-heavy functions.
• Blank identifier _: discards a value without allocation; silences unused-import/variable errors.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
• 'What's the difference between a slice and an array in Go?' — leads into value vs reference.
• 'What is the zero value of a map? Can you read from a nil map?' — yes, read returns zero; write panics.
• 'When would you use a pointer receiver vs a value receiver?' — mutation, large structs, interface consistency.
• 'What does iota do and give a real-world example.' — bitmask flags, log levels, weekdays.
• 'Can you compare two structs with ==?' — only if all fields are comparable (no slices/maps/funcs).

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "In Go, the key mental shift is value-vs-reference semantics. When I assign a struct, I get a full copy, which is great for immutability but means mutations don't propagate. When I assign a slice or map I'm copying the header — both variables point at the same backing array or hash table. I always think about zero values first: every Go variable starts at a well-defined zero, so I don't need nil checks the way I would in Java. With pointers I'm explicit — I take an address when I need to share mutation or avoid copying a large struct, and I use the two-value type-assertion form to avoid panics when asserting on an interface."
